pages.text: Pick up a pen. Your brain sends a signal. Twenty-nine muscles in your hand and forearm contract and relax in precise, coordinated sequence. Bones pivot at joints. Tendons transmit force from muscle to bone. Ligaments hold joints stable. You pick up the pen. This action, which takes less than a second, involves more biological coordination than any human-made machine has ever replicated. And you do not have to think about any of it.

image.note: Illustration: the human skeleton in full, front view, with key bones labelled

pages.text: The human skeleton contains 206 bones in an adult. Babies are born with approximately 270 bones; many fuse together as the body develops. The skeleton is not decoration or simply a frame. It produces red blood cells in the marrow inside the larger bones. It stores minerals, particularly calcium and phosphorus, releasing them into the bloodstream when the body needs them. It protects vital organs: the skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs.

Bone is living tissue. It is constantly being broken down and rebuilt by two types of cell: osteoclasts, which dissolve old bone, and osteoblasts, which build new bone. Over the course of several years, most of the skeleton is replaced. This means that the bones of a healthy adult are not the same physical material they were seven years ago, even though they are in the same position and roughly the same shape.

Bone is one of nature's finest materials, stronger for its weight than steel or concrete, yet light enough to run on. The secret is a partnership: hard mineral crystals give bone its stiffness, while stretchy fibres of a protein called collagen give it the flex to absorb a blow without shattering. Too much mineral and a bone would snap like chalk; too little and it would bend like rubber. Bone is the perfect compromise.

Bone is one of the most sophisticated structural materials in nature. Its outer layer is dense, hard cortical bone, providing strength and rigidity. The interior contains trabecular bone, a lightweight lattice of struts and spaces that is arranged along the lines of greatest mechanical stress, like an internal scaffolding. This combination of a hard shell and an internal lattice gives bone an extraordinary ratio of strength to weight.

image.note: Cross-section diagram of a long bone showing cortical bone, trabecular bone interior, and bone marrow cavity

pages.text: The skeleton is not rigid. It is a system of levers, connected at joints, that allows an enormous range of movement. Different joints allow different types of movement. Ball-and-socket joints, like the hip and shoulder, allow movement in all directions. Hinge joints, like the knee and elbow, allow movement in one plane only. Pivot joints, like the joint at the top of the neck, allow rotation.

Between the bones at most joints is a layer of cartilage: smooth, firm, slightly compressible tissue that cushions the joint and allows bones to glide against each other without friction. Joint fluid, secreted by the joint lining, lubricates the joint further. When cartilage is damaged or worn away, as in arthritis, bones rub directly against each other, causing pain and restricting movement.

Bones are alive and always at work. Deep inside the large bones, red marrow runs a factory that produces millions of new blood cells every second of your life. Bones also act as the body's mineral bank, storing calcium and releasing it into the blood when the heart, nerves, and muscles need it. And when a bone breaks, it does something steel cannot: it heals itself, knitting the pieces back into a single living whole.

Your ear holds three of the strangest bones in your body. The hammer, anvil, and stirrup, the smallest bones you own, sit in a chain in the middle ear, passing sound vibrations from the eardrum inward. The stirrup is smaller than a grain of rice. Without these three tiny bones, the world would fall almost silent. Engineering does not get more delicate, and evolution built it in the dark.

The human body has more than 600 muscles. They range in size from the gluteus maximus, the large muscle of the buttock that powers walking, running, and climbing, to the stapedius, a tiny muscle in the middle ear barely one millimetre long, that dampens the vibration of the ossicles to protect hearing from loud sounds.

Muscles work by contracting: shortening and thickening as millions of protein filaments inside the muscle cells slide past each other. They cannot push; they can only pull. This means that most movements require two opposing muscles or muscle groups: one to produce the movement, and another to reverse it. The bicep, which bends the arm at the elbow, is paired with the tricep, which straightens it.

image.note: Diagram showing bicep and tricep in opposition during arm bending and straightening

pages.text: There are three types of muscle in the body. Skeletal muscle, attached to bones and under voluntary control, is what most people mean when they say the word muscle. Cardiac muscle, found only in the heart, contracts automatically and never stops. Smooth muscle, found in the walls of blood vessels, the gut, and other internal organs, operates automatically, moving food through the digestive system, controlling blood pressure, and performing dozens of other functions without any conscious instruction.

Muscles adapt to the demands placed on them. Regular resistance exercise causes muscle fibres to grow thicker and stronger. This is why athletes who train consistently develop significantly more muscle mass than people who are sedentary. Conversely, muscles that are not used shrink: an arm immobilised in a cast for six weeks will emerge visibly thinner than the other arm.

Muscles come in three kinds, and you command only one. Skeletal muscle, which moves your bones, obeys your will. But cardiac muscle drives your heart, and smooth muscle pushes food through your gut, widens and narrows blood vessels, and works in dozens of organs, all without a single conscious command. Right now, muscles you cannot feel are keeping you alive. The muscles you can control are a small, visible fraction of the whole team.

chapters.title: Caring for Your Skeleton and Muscles

pages.text: The skeleton built in childhood and adolescence is the skeleton that must last a lifetime. Peak bone density is reached in the mid-twenties. After that, the balance between bone formation and bone resorption gradually shifts, and bone density slowly declines. Building as much bone density as possible during childhood, through good nutrition and regular exercise, is the best way to protect against fractures and osteoporosis in later life.

Calcium and vitamin D are the most important nutrients for bone health. Calcium is the primary mineral in bone. Vitamin D is needed for the body to absorb calcium from food. In Nigeria, vitamin D deficiency is less common than in countries with less sunlight, because the body produces vitamin D when skin is exposed to sunlight. However, rickets, a childhood bone disease caused by vitamin D and calcium deficiency, remains a significant health issue in some parts of northern Nigeria.

Physical activity strengthens both bone and muscle. Weight-bearing exercise, exercise in which the skeleton bears the body's weight, such as walking, running, jumping, and dancing, is particularly effective at building bone density. Exercise also builds muscle, which in turn supports and protects the joints, reducing the risk of injury.

image.note: Illustration of children playing football, with inset showing stressed bone responding by building density

pages.text: The body that carries you through your life is built from the food you eat, the exercise you do, and the rest you give it. Understanding how bones and muscles work is understanding the physical machine you live in. It is a remarkable machine. It is worth understanding, and worth looking after.

This system is built to be built. Bones grow stronger when they are loaded, so running, jumping, dancing, and climbing lay down denser bone that lasts a lifetime. Muscles grow with use and shrink with idleness. Good food supplies the raw materials: calcium and protein to build, vitamin D, which sunlight helps your skin make, to lock the calcium in. The active, well-fed body of childhood is the foundation of a strong body decades later.
